summary: This work develops a three-dimensional Schrödinger–Poisson framework to model electron trapping on solid neon and proposes engineering the dielectric substrate surface to enable deterministic single-electron confinement. The simulations demonstrate that nanoscale surface roughness (bumps and valleys with $\sigma_{\mathrm{rms}} = 3$ nm) substantially perturbs the trapping landscape, but a combination of a planarizing dielectric spacer and selective etching creates controlled potential minima while suppressing parasitic bound states.
motivation: Levitating electrons on solid neon offer long coherence times (approaching 93 μs for charge qubits) and escape conventional decoherence channels, but deterministic electron loading and precise positioning remain unsolved challenges. Unintended trapping by surface roughness, resonator gaps, and substrate features introduces charge noise and decoherence.
method: A three-dimensional Schrödinger–Poisson solver on a $121 \times 121 \times 111$ mesh was used to compute orbital eigenstates and energies for different device geometries: smooth gates, rough surfaces with $\pm 3$ nm perturbations, gates with dielectric spacers of variable thickness $H$, and dielectric with selective etched trenches. The model was validated against experimental orbital splittings of $\Delta E \approx 6.3$–$6.4$ GHz.
result: A continuous dielectric layer (with $\epsilon_r \approx 3.5$) planarizes the surface and eliminates roughness-induced trapping that would shift $\Delta E$ from 6.2 GHz to 10.6 GHz; selective etching of the dielectric recovers $\Delta E \approx 6.1$ GHz while creating deterministic confinement, demonstrating a practical route to scalable, reproducible electron positioning on solid neon.
